description: just gonna build things from scratch
summary:
Lunar Navigator, developed by Team EpochSwarm, is a decision-support prototype that helps evaluate potential lunar landing opportunities at the Moon’s south pole. It addresses the challenge of limited sunlight and intermittent Earth communication, where crater rims and uneven terrain can determine whether a site supports power, communication, both, or neither.

Using NASA LOLA 80 m terrain data and NAIF SPICE (DE440) ephemerides, the system calculates hourly Sun and Earth visibility, compares nine Artemis III candidate regions, and ranks 14-day mission windows. It also explores how antenna and panel height affect visibility and uses Monte Carlo simulations to quantify uncertainty through confidence bands and robustness labels. An interactive 3D environment and plain-English Copilot make these analyses easier to explore.

Validated against analytical ephemeris calculations and published lunar illumination results, Lunar Navigator turns complex scientific data into an accessible view of mission opportunities and their reliability. It is designed to support exploration by mission planners, students, and the public, while clearly distinguishing representative site points from certified landing coordinates.
details:
Lunar Navigator answers the question mission planners face at the Moon’s south pole: can a site support a mission, when, and how sure are we?

The problem. From the south pole the Sun and Earth sit only a few degrees above the horizon. A single crater rim can decide whether a lander gets solar power, a direct-to-Earth link, both, or neither, and the answer changes hour by hour.

What it does. Lunar Navigator compares NASA’s nine Artemis III candidate regions on real terrain. It computes hourly Sun and Earth visibility, ranks 14-day mission windows, tests how antenna and panel height changes the result, and quantifies uncertainty. Users can explore each site in an interactive 3D dome (orbit, lander and top-down views) with live Sun and Earth sightlines. A plain-English Copilot answers planning questions.

How it works. We ray-march horizon profiles over NASA LOLA 80 m terrain, with lunar curvature included. We compute Sun and Earth positions with NAIF SPICE (DE440) and classify each hour as power, link, both, or neither. A mast-height sweep finds “rim flips”, where a few metres of height clear a ridge. A Monte Carlo analysis (30 runs of correlated terrain-height noise) gives P10-P90 confidence bands and a Robust / Moderate / Fragile label for each window. The Copilot’s answers are checked by a deterministic verifier that rejects any number not present in the computed results.

Validation. SPICE agrees with our analytical ephemeris to within 0.006° across 864 samples. Our illumination results match published values from Mazarico et al. (2011): Shackleton crater floor at 0% illumination and Malapert at about 42% Earth visibility. 65 automated tests pass.

Impact. It turns scattered terrain and ephemeris data into a decision view that shows both the answer and how much to trust it. It’s useful for mission planners and also for students and the public, via a Planner/Public mode.

Tools. Python, NumPy, SciPy, SpiceyPy, an ASGI server (Uvicorn), vanilla JavaScript, Canvas 2D and Three.js (WebGL), with no build step.

Limitations we state openly. The nine points are representative region centroids, not certified landing coordinates. Our terrain-error model is deliberately conservative (8 m vs about 1.5 m real), and rankings did not change at either value.
